summary: This RFC introduces a series of specifications for fully supporting internationalized email addresses. Users should be able to use mailbox names in their own language and script. It describes the changes and protocol extensions needed across mail systems.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains a set of changes that let email use UTF-8 addresses and header information. The changes cover sending, delivery notices and access to messages, so systems can handle the new format consistently.

questions: can email addresses use non-ascii characters
subtitle: Framework for email addresses and headers that use UTF-8 across mail systems.

tldr.problem: Email domains can use internationalized names, but mailbox local parts and traditional headers are limited in ways that exclude many scripts.
tldr.mechanism: A group of specifications extends SMTP for UTF-8 addresses, permits UTF-8 in headers and adapts delivery notifications and retrieval protocols.
tldr.outcome: This RFC provides the framework, removes in-transit downgrading and obsoletes RFCs 4952, 5504 and 5825.

today: RFC 6530 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4952, RFC 5504 and RFC 5825. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Email Addresses Need UTF-8
sections.content:
An email address has a local part and a domain part. Domain names can already be internationalized, but traditional email restricts the local part to a subset of 7-bit ASCII. MIME can carry non-ASCII message data, but it does not make non-ASCII characters part of an address.

The RFC argues that changing only one part of email would leave inconsistent systems. Address handling, message headers, transport and delivery notices need compatible changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the domain name alone does not let people write the mailbox name in their own script. Email systems need coordinated changes to addresses, headers and delivery.

sections.title: Conventional and Internationalized Messages
sections.content:
The RFC calls an address all-ASCII when every character belongs to ASCII; an address with any other character is non-ASCII. SMTPUTF8 is the umbrella term for this email internationalization work.

A conventional message uses none of the new extensions and follows RFC 5322. An internationalized message uses one or more extensions and no longer follows the traditional message and transport rules exactly.
sections.plainLanguage: A message is internationalized when it uses one of the new address or header features. Older mail systems may not understand those features.

sections.title: The Internationalized Email Specification Set
sections.content:
This RFC is the framework for a set of specifications. RFC 6531 extends SMTP for internationalized addresses, RFC 6532 permits UTF-8 in selected header fields, and RFC 6533 adapts delivery and disposition notifications. The framework also discusses planned support for IMAP and POP.

SMTPUTF8 permits UTF-8 in local parts and domain names and requires 8BITMIME support. When an SMTP relay cannot accept the extension, it must reject the message or return a non-delivery notification rather than silently pass it onward.
sections.plainLanguage: One document covers sending, another covers headers and another covers delivery notices. The set gives mail systems shared rules for handling UTF-8 addresses.

sections.title: Downgrading and Legacy Systems
sections.content:
ASCII-only systems can send to internationalized systems because ASCII addresses remain part of the supported set. A sender may need to use conventional addresses and headers or ask the user to change the message when the first server does not support SMTPUTF8.

The RFC says a message cannot be downgraded in transit by changing its local-part address. Only an endpoint, such as the sending user agent or final delivery system, can make that change. A final delivery system that downgrades a message should preserve a way to recover the original information.
sections.plainLanguage: Systems that do not support UTF-8 need a conventional form of the message. The RFC places any address conversion at the sending or final-delivery end, not at an intermediate relay.

sections.title: Naming, Security and Lessons from Experiments
sections.content:
Different characters can look alike, so internationalized local parts can enable address spoofing. The RFC also warns that filters and mail programs may interpret malformed messages differently, and that transformations can affect signed headers.

Earlier experiments allowed in-transit downgrading and paired non-ASCII addresses with ASCII alternatives. Interoperability problems and security concerns led the working group to remove that approach. The unit metadata says this RFC obsoletes RFC 4952, RFC 5504 and RFC 5825.
sections.plainLanguage: Look-alike characters can make a misleading address appear genuine. The revised approach removes in-transit conversion because it caused security and interoperability problems.

viz.caption: MAIN PARTS OF THE INTERNATIONALIZED EMAIL WORK

items.title: SMTP
items.text: Carries internationalized addresses and message data.

items.title: Headers
items.text: Allows UTF-8 in selected header fields.

items.title: Notifications
items.text: Preserves internationalized addresses in delivery notices.

items.title: Message access
items.text: The framework identifies IMAP and POP as parts of the wider work.
